blocks.body:
Put $n$ points in the plane. How many pairs can be at distance exactly 1? How few different distances can the pairs determine? Must some of the points form a convex pentagon? Must some line pass through exactly two of them? Combinatorial geometry asks such questions about finite configurations of points, lines and circles, where the answer depends on both counting and geometry.

Many of these problems were posed by Erdős in the 1930s and 1940s. The best answers combine double counting, graph drawing, Ramsey theory and, since 2010, algebraic geometry.

blocks.title: Unit distances and distinct distances
blocks.body:
For a set $P$ of $n$ points, let $u(P)$ be the number of pairs at distance 1 and $g(P)$ the number of distinct distances among all pairs. Write $u(n)$ for the maximum of $u(P)$ and $g(n)$ for the minimum of $g(P)$ over $n$-point sets. The two problems pull in opposite directions: a set with few distinct distances must repeat some distance often.

Simple constructions. Points equally spaced on a line, at $0, 1, \dots, n-1$, give $n - 1$ unit distances and $n - 1$ distinct distances. Doing better takes more care. A square $\sqrt n \times \sqrt n$ grid of integer points determines only about $n/\sqrt{\log n}$ distinct distances, because the squared distances are sums of two squares below $2n$, and few integers have that form (see [[sums-of-squares]]). Scaling the same grid so that its most frequent distance becomes 1, Erdős obtained $u(n) \ge n^{1 + c/\log\log n}$ for a constant $c > 0$.

Elementary upper and lower bounds come from the fact that two distinct circles meet in at most two points.

blocks.title: Elementary distance bounds

blocks.body:
1. For each point $p$, let $d_p$ be the number of points at distance 1 from $p$; then $\sum_p d_p = 2u$. Count triples $(p, \{q, r\})$ with $q, r$ both at distance 1 from $p$. For fixed $p$ there are $\binom{d_p}{2}$ of them. For a fixed pair $\{q, r\}$, the point $p$ lies on the unit circles around $q$ and around $r$, which meet in at most two points. So
$$\sum_p \binom{d_p}{2} \le 2\binom n2 = n(n-1).$$
The function $x \mapsto x(x-1)/2$ is convex, so with $x = 2u/n$ the average degree, $\sum_p \binom{d_p}{2} \ge n\cdot\frac{x(x-1)}{2}$ (see [[convexity]]). Hence $x^2 - x - 2(n-1) \le 0$, so $x \le \frac12\big(1 + \sqrt{8n-7}\big)$ and $u = nx/2 \le \frac n4\big(1 + \sqrt{8n-7}\big)$.

2. Let the distinct distances be $r_1, \dots, r_t$ and fix two points $p \ne q$. Each of the other $n - 2$ points lies on one of the $t$ circles of radius $r_i$ around $p$ and on one of the $t$ circles of radius $r_j$ around $q$. For each of the $t^2$ choices of $(i, j)$ the two circles have different centres and meet in at most 2 points. So $n - 2 \le 2t^2$.

blocks.title: What is known, and a 2026 claim
blocks.body:
Both elementary bounds are far from the truth.

For unit distances, Spencer, Szemerédi and Trotter proved in 1984 that
$$\#\text{unit distances} \le O(n^{4/3}).$$
Székely (1997) found a short proof via the crossing lemma: a graph drawn in the plane with $v$ vertices and $e \ge 4v$ edges has at least $e^3/(64v^2)$ pairs of crossing edges. Applying it to the drawing whose edges are arcs of the unit circles around the points gives the $n^{4/3}$ bound (details omitted). The exponent $4/3$ has not been improved since 1984.

Erdős conjectured in 1946 that his grid construction is close to optimal: $u(n)$ is at most $n^{1+o(1)}$, and in a sharper form of order $n^{1 + c/\log\log n}$, like the grid. Claim (May 2026): on 20 May 2026 a counterexample to Erdős's unit distance conjecture was reported, found by an internal OpenAI model; Tim Gowers is reported to have praised the proof. This is a claim, not yet an established result, and this lesson does not rely on it or describe what bound it gives.

For distinct distances, Erdős conjectured that the grid is optimal up to constants, $g(n) \ge c\,n/\sqrt{\log n}$. In 2010 Guth and Katz proved
$$\#\text{distinct distances} \ge c\,\frac{n}{\log n},$$
which misses the conjecture by only a factor $\sqrt{\log n}$. Following an idea of Elekes and Sharir, they turn the problem into counting intersecting pairs of lines in three-dimensional space, and bound those by polynomial partitioning: the zero set of a polynomial of controlled degree cuts space into cells each meeting few lines.

blocks.title: Incidences between points and lines
blocks.body: An incidence between a set of points and a set of lines is a pair (point, line) with the point on the line. With $m$ points and $n$ lines, a Cauchy–Schwarz argument gives at most about $m\sqrt n + n$ incidences (third example). The truth is smaller.

blocks.title: Szemerédi–Trotter theorem (1983)
blocks.body:
There is a constant $C$ such that $m$ points and $n$ lines in the plane have at most
$$C\big(m^{2/3}n^{2/3} + m + n\big)$$
incidences.

blocks.title: About the Szemerédi–Trotter theorem
blocks.body: The proof is omitted; Székely's crossing-lemma argument gives it in a page. The bound is sharp up to the constant: with points the integer grid $\{1,\dots,k\} \times \{1,\dots,2k^2\}$ and lines $y = ax + b$ with $a \in \{1,\dots,k\}$, $b \in \{1,\dots,k^2\}$, each line contains $k$ grid points, giving $k^4$ incidences among $2k^3$ points and $k^3$ lines, which is of order $m^{2/3}n^{2/3}$. Unit distances are an incidence problem between points and unit circles, which is why the same exponent $4/3$ appears.

blocks.title: Convex position: the Erdős–Szekeres theorem
blocks.body: A set of points is in general position if no three are collinear, and in convex position if each point is a vertex of the convex hull of the set. Esther Klein observed that among any 5 points in general position, 4 are in convex position (second example). Erdős and Szekeres asked how many points force $k$ points in convex position; the story is known as the happy ending problem, because Klein and Szekeres later married.

blocks.title: Erdős–Szekeres theorem (1935)
blocks.body:
For every $k \ge 3$ there is a least integer $f(k)$ such that every set of $f(k)$ points in general position in the plane contains $k$ points in convex position. Moreover
$$2^{k-2} + 1 \le f(k) \le \binom{2k-4}{k-2} + 1.$$

blocks.title: Proof that f(k) exists
blocks.body:
We prove existence using Ramsey's theorem for 4-element subsets (see [[ramsey]]); the explicit bounds need finer arguments and are not proved here.

First, if every 4 points of a finite set $S$ in general position are in convex position, then $S$ is in convex position. Otherwise some point $p \in S$ is not a vertex of the convex hull of $S$, so it lies in that hull. Triangulate the hull by joining one hull vertex to all others; $p$ lies in one of these triangles, whose vertices are three points of $S$, and by general position it is in the interior. Those three points together with $p$ are not in convex position.

Now colour each 4-element subset of a large point set red if it is in convex position and blue otherwise. By Ramsey's theorem there is an $N$ such that any such colouring of the 4-subsets of $N$ points has a 5-set all of whose 4-subsets are blue or a $k$-set all of whose 4-subsets are red. The first is impossible by Klein's observation. So there are $k$ points all of whose 4-subsets are convex, and by the previous paragraph they are in convex position.

blocks.title: The current state
blocks.body: The lower bound $2^{k-2} + 1$ comes from an explicit construction of Erdős and Szekeres (1961), who conjectured it is exact. Small cases agree: $f(4) = 5$ by Klein's observation, $f(5) = 9$, and $f(6) = 17$, the last by a computer search of Szekeres and Peters (2006). In 2017 Andrew Suk proved $f(k) \le 2^{k + o(k)}$, so the conjecture is now known to be right in the exponent.

blocks.title: Sylvester–Gallai theorem
blocks.body: If a finite set of points in the plane is not contained in a line, then some line passes through exactly two of the points.

blocks.title: Kelly's proof
blocks.body:
Call a line connecting if it passes through at least two of the points. Consider all pairs $(P, \ell)$ where $\ell$ is a connecting line and $P$ is a point of the set not on $\ell$; such pairs exist because the points are not collinear, and there are finitely many. Choose a pair for which the distance from $P$ to $\ell$ is smallest, and let $Q$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $\ell$.

Suppose $\ell$ contains at least three of the points. The point $Q$ divides $\ell$ into two closed rays, so by [[pigeonhole]] two of the points, $A$ and $B$, lie on the same ray; name them so that $|QB| \le |QA|$. Then $A \ne Q$ and $B$ lies on the segment $QA$ (possibly $B = Q$).

Let $m$ be the connecting line $PA$. The point $B$ is not on $m$, since otherwise $m$ would be $\ell$ and $P$ would lie on $\ell$. As a point moves along the segment from $Q$ to $A$, its distance to the line $PA$ decreases in proportion to its distance from $A$, so the distance from $B$ to $m$ is at most the distance from $Q$ to $m$. In the right triangle $PQA$, the distance from $Q$ to the hypotenuse $PA$ equals $|PQ|\cdot|QA|/|PA|$, and $|QA| < |PA|$, so this distance is less than $|PQ|$. Hence the pair $(B, m)$ has smaller distance than $(P, \ell)$, a contradiction. So $\ell$ contains exactly two of the points.

blocks.title: Many unit distances from a cube
blocks.body: Show that for every $k$ there is a set of $n = 2^k$ points in the plane with at least $k\,2^{k-1} = \frac n2 \log_2 n$ unit distances. So $u(n)$ grows faster than any linear function.
blocks.solution:
Choose unit vectors $v_1, \dots, v_k$ in the plane and, for each subset $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, k\}$, the point $x_S = \sum_{i \in S} v_i$. If the directions are chosen generically (for instance at random), the $2^k$ points $x_S$ are distinct, since a coincidence $x_S = x_T$ is a nontrivial linear relation among the $v_i$ with coefficients $0, \pm 1$, and each such relation fails for almost every choice.

If $T = S \cup \{i\}$ with $i \notin S$, then $x_T - x_S = v_i$ has length 1. Each of the $2^k$ subsets $T$ has $|T|$ such neighbours $S$ below it, so the number of these pairs is $\sum_T |T| = k\,2^{k-1}$. All of them are unit distances (there may be more).

This is the planar shadow of the $k$-dimensional cube, whose $k\,2^{k-1}$ edges all have the same length.

blocks.title: Klein's five-point lemma
blocks.body: Prove that among any 5 points in the plane, no three collinear, some 4 are the vertices of a convex quadrilateral.
blocks.solution:
Look at the convex hull. If it has 5 or 4 vertices, any 4 hull vertices are in convex position.

Otherwise the hull is a triangle $ABC$ and the other two points $D$, $E$ lie inside it. The line $DE$ passes through no vertex of the triangle (no three points are collinear), so it leaves the three vertices on its two sides, and by pigeonhole two of them, say $A$ and $B$, are on the same side.

We claim $A, B, D, E$ are in convex position, that is, none of them lies inside the triangle of the other three. $A$ is a vertex of triangle $ABC$, which contains $B$, $D$ and $E$, so $A$ cannot lie in the triangle $BDE$; similarly for $B$. If $D$ were inside triangle $ABE$, the line from the vertex $E$ through the interior point $D$ would cross the opposite side $AB$ at an interior point of the segment, putting $A$ and $B$ on opposite sides of line $DE$, contrary to the choice of $A$, $B$. The same argument with $D$ and $E$ exchanged rules out $E$ inside $ABD$. So $ABDE$ (in a suitable order) is a convex quadrilateral.

Four points are not enough: a triangle with one point inside has no convex quadrilateral.

blocks.title: A first incidence bound
blocks.body: Show that $m$ points and $n$ lines in the plane have at most $n + m\sqrt n$ incidences.
blocks.solution:
For each line $\ell$ let $d_\ell$ be the number of points on it, so the number of incidences is $I = \sum_\ell d_\ell$. Count ordered pairs of distinct points lying on a common line: line $\ell$ contributes $d_\ell(d_\ell - 1)$, and each ordered pair of points lies on at most one line, so
$$\sum_\ell d_\ell^2 - I = \sum_\ell d_\ell(d_\ell - 1) \le m(m-1) \le m^2.$$
By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality (see [[cauchy-schwarz]]), $I^2 = \big(\sum_\ell d_\ell\big)^2 \le n\sum_\ell d_\ell^2 \le n(m^2 + I)$. Thus $I^2 - nI - nm^2 \le 0$, and
$$I \le \frac{n + \sqrt{n^2 + 4nm^2}}{2} \le \frac{n + (n + 2m\sqrt n)}{2} = n + m\sqrt n,$$
using $n^2 + 4nm^2 \le (n + 2m\sqrt n)^2$. For $m = n$ this gives $O(n^{3/2})$, compared with the true order $n^{4/3}$ from Szemerédi–Trotter.

blocks.body:
- Unit-distance and distinct-distance problems point in opposite directions, but they are linked: any distance can be scaled to 1, so each distance occurs at most $u(n)$ times and $g(n) \ge \binom n2 / u(n)$. With the $O(n^{4/3})$ bound this already gives $g(n) \ge c\,n^{2/3}$, far better than the elementary $\sqrt n$.
- General position matters. Without it, all $n$ points could lie on a line, which contains no convex quadrilateral at all.
- The Sylvester–Gallai theorem is special to real geometry and finite sets. Over the complex numbers it fails (the 9 inflection points of a smooth plane cubic have every connecting line through 3 of them), and it fails for infinite sets such as the integer lattice.
- A reported proof is not an accepted one; recent claims, including AI-generated ones, should be cited as claims until independently checked.

- [[ramsey]]: the Erdős–Szekeres theorem is one of the earliest applications of Ramsey's theorem.
- [[probabilistic-method]]: the crossing lemma, behind Székely's proofs, has a short probabilistic proof.
- [[additive-combinatorics]]: Elekes used the Szemerédi–Trotter theorem to prove the sum-product estimate $\max(|A+A|, |A\cdot A|) \ge c|A|^{5/4}$ for finite sets of reals.
- [[sums-of-squares]]: the distinct distances of a grid are governed by which integers are sums of two squares.
- [[hypergraphs]]: points and lines form a linear hypergraph, and incidence bounds are extremal results for it.
- [[polynomials-roots]]: the polynomial method rests on simple facts such as: a polynomial of degree $d$ vanishing at $d+1$ points of a line vanishes on the whole line.

1. Show that the vertices of a regular $n$-gon determine exactly $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ distinct distances.
2. Prove that 4 points in the plane determine at most 5 unit distances, and find 4 points with exactly 5.
3. Show that $m$ points and $n$ lines have at most $m + n\sqrt m$ incidences, by exchanging the roles of points and lines in the third example.
4. Show that the Sylvester–Gallai theorem fails for the infinite set $\mathbb Z^2$ of integer points: every line through two of them contains infinitely many.

sources.ref: Guth & Katz, On the Erdős distinct distances problem in the plane, Annals of Mathematics 181 (2015)
